0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance

Random variables and scenario tables

Section titled “Random variables and scenario tables”

A quantity whose value is uncertain, but whose possible values and their probabilities are known, is called a random variable. The return of an investment is a random variable.

Here is an example: the annual returns (%) of stock A and bond fund B in three economic scenarios.

ScenarioProbability pppStock ABond fund B
Boom0.25301
Normal0.50105
Recession0.25−103

The probabilities of all scenarios must add up to 1. In reality we do not know the true probabilities; this table is a simplified model. How to estimate these quantities from historical data, and how large the estimation error can be, is covered in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference.

Expected value

Section titled “Expected value”

The expected value is the average result if the same situation is repeated many times. It is computed as a probability-weighted average:

E[R]=∑ipiRiE[R] = \sum_i p_i R_iE[R]=i∑​pi​Ri​

For stock A:

E[RA]=0.25×30+0.5×10+0.25×(−10)=10%E[R_A] = 0.25 \times 30 + 0.5 \times 10 + 0.25 \times (-10) = 10\%E[RA​]=0.25×30+0.5×10+0.25×(−10)=10%
Check C1
Use the same method to calculate the expected return of B. Show the calculation.

Variance and standard deviation

Section titled “Variance and standard deviation”

The expected value alone is not enough: two investments can have the same expected value but very different spreads of outcomes. We want to measure how far the outcomes are from the expected value. Deviations can be positive or negative, and a plain average of them is always 0, so we square them first and then take the probability-weighted average. This gives the variance. The square root of the variance is the standard deviation:

Var(R)=∑ipi(Ri−E[R])2,σ=Var(R)\text{Var}(R) = \sum_i p_i \big(R_i - E[R]\big)^2, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\text{Var}(R)}Var(R)=i∑​pi​(Ri​−E[R])2,σ=Var(R)​

For A, the deviations from the expected value in the three scenarios are +20, 0 and −20:

Var(RA)=0.25×202+0.5×02+0.25×(−20)2=200\text{Var}(R_A) = 0.25 \times 20^2 + 0.5 \times 0^2 + 0.25 \times (-20)^2 = 200Var(RA​)=0.25×202+0.5×02+0.25×(−20)2=200

So σA=200≈14.14%\sigma_A = \sqrt{200} \approx 14.14\%σA​=200​≈14.14%. In the same way, the variance of B is 2.75 (%²) and σB≈1.66%\sigma_B \approx 1.66\%σB​≈1.66%.

Units: the unit of variance is %², which has no intuitive meaning. The standard deviation is back in %, so it can be compared directly with the expected return. “Volatility” in finance means the standard deviation. Also note that squaring makes large deviations count more: a deviation of 20 contributes 100 times as much as a deviation of 2.

Check C2
If A's return in every scenario increases by 5 percentage points, how do its expected value and standard deviation change? Why?

Covariance and correlation

Section titled “Covariance and correlation”

The risk of a portfolio depends not only on how much each asset varies, but also on whether the assets vary together. This is measured by the covariance:

Cov(RA,RB)=∑ipi(RA,i−E[RA])(RB,i−E[RB])\text{Cov}(R_A, R_B) = \sum_i p_i \big(R_{A,i} - E[R_A]\big)\big(R_{B,i} - E[R_B]\big)Cov(RA​,RB​)=i∑​pi​(RA,i​−E[RA​])(RB,i​−E[RB​])

In a scenario where both are above or both are below their own expected values, the product is positive. If one is above and the other is below, the product is negative.

ScenariopppA deviationB deviationProduct
Boom0.25+20−2.5−50
Normal0.500+1.50
Recession0.25−20−0.5+10

The probability-weighted sum is Cov=0.25×(−50)+0.5×0+0.25×10=−10\text{Cov} = 0.25 \times (-50) + 0.5 \times 0 + 0.25 \times 10 = -10Cov=0.25×(−50)+0.5×0+0.25×10=−10 (%²).

The size of the covariance depends on the units, so it is hard to compare. Dividing it by the two standard deviations gives the correlation coefficient:

ρAB=Cov(RA,RB)σAσB≈−1014.14×1.66≈−0.43\rho_{AB} = \frac{\text{Cov}(R_A, R_B)}{\sigma_A \sigma_B} \approx \frac{-10}{14.14 \times 1.66} \approx -0.43ρAB​=σA​σB​Cov(RA​,RB​)​≈14.14×1.66−10​≈−0.43

The correlation coefficient has no unit and lies in [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1]. It measures only linear relationships, and correlation does not imply causation (correlation and causation).

Check C3
If B's return in the recession scenario changes from 3% to 8% (everything else unchanged), does the covariance become larger or smaller? First judge by intuition, then verify by calculation.

Expected value and variance of a linear combination

Section titled “Expected value and variance of a linear combination”

Now split your money into two parts: a fraction www in A and a fraction 1−w1 - w1−w in B. The portfolio return is RP=wRA+(1−w)RBR_P = wR_A + (1-w)R_BRP​=wRA​+(1−w)RB​.

The expected value is linear:

E[RP]=w E[RA]+(1−w) E[RB]E[R_P] = w\,E[R_A] + (1-w)\,E[R_B]E[RP​]=wE[RA​]+(1−w)E[RB​]

But the variance is not linear. The portfolio variance has an extra covariance term:

Var(RP)=w2σA2+(1−w)2σB2+2w(1−w) Cov(RA,RB)\text{Var}(R_P) = w^2\sigma_A^2 + (1-w)^2\sigma_B^2 + 2w(1-w)\,\text{Cov}(R_A, R_B)Var(RP​)=w2σA2​+(1−w)2σB2​+2w(1−w)Cov(RA​,RB​)

This formula is the core of 4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory (not yet published).

Example: 50% in A and 50% in B.

  • E[RP]=0.5×10+0.5×3.5=6.75%E[R_P] = 0.5 \times 10 + 0.5 \times 3.5 = 6.75\%E[RP​]=0.5×10+0.5×3.5=6.75%.
  • Var(RP)=0.25×200+0.25×2.75+2×0.25×(−10)=45.69\text{Var}(R_P) = 0.25 \times 200 + 0.25 \times 2.75 + 2 \times 0.25 \times (-10) = 45.69Var(RP​)=0.25×200+0.25×2.75+2×0.25×(−10)=45.69 (%²), so σP≈6.76%\sigma_P \approx 6.76\%σP​≈6.76%.
  • Check: the portfolio returns in the three scenarios are 15.5, 7.5 and −3.5. Computing the variance directly from these three numbers gives the same result.

The weighted average of the standard deviations is 0.5×14.14+0.5×1.66=7.90%0.5 \times 14.14 + 0.5 \times 1.66 = 7.90\%0.5×14.14+0.5×1.66=7.90%, but the actual portfolio standard deviation is only 6.76%6.76\%6.76%. Why is it smaller? That is the topic of the next section. The derivation of this formula is left as Exercises Question 5.

Check C4
With 80% in A and 20% in B, what are the portfolio's expected value and standard deviation?

Diversification

Section titled “Diversification”

Rewrite the portfolio variance with the correlation coefficient:

σP2=w2σA2+(1−w)2σB2+2w(1−w)ρ σAσB\sigma_P^2 = w^2\sigma_A^2 + (1-w)^2\sigma_B^2 + 2w(1-w)\rho\,\sigma_A\sigma_BσP2​=w2σA2​+(1−w)2σB2​+2w(1−w)ρσA​σB​

When the portfolio standard deviation is lower than the weighted average of the standard deviations of the assets, we say that the portfolio benefits from diversification. What happens for different values of the correlation? First explore it with the figure below. In reality, the correlation between most assets is between 0 and 1.

Set ρ\rhoρ to 0 and find the approximate weight that minimizes the portfolio standard deviation. Is the portfolio standard deviation then smaller than B's own 10%? What does this show?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Expected value: the probability-weighted average. Variance: the probability-weighted average of squared deviations (%²). Standard deviation: the square root of the variance (%).
  • Covariance: positive when the deviations from each expected value have the same direction, negative when they have opposite directions. Correlation coefficient: the covariance scaled to [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1].
  • The expected value of a portfolio is a weighted average; the variance of a portfolio has an extra covariance term and is not a weighted average.
